name: Milwaukee shoulder syndrome
aliases: BCP destructive arthropathy of the shoulder

clinicalPearls: Milwaukee shoulder is a rapidly destructive arthropathy of the shoulder driven by basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals, typically affecting elderly women
It presents with a large, often blood-tinged, minimally inflammatory joint effusion together with shoulder pain and marked loss of function
There is extensive rotator cuff deficiency (a large or massive tear) that allows superior migration of the humeral head towards the acromion
Radiographs show glenohumeral joint destruction, superior subluxation of the humeral head into a high-riding position, and soft-tissue calcification

Synovial fluid contains relatively few cells (non-inflammatory to only mildly inflammatory) but harbours aggregates of BCP crystals, which are non-birefringent and require special staining such as alizarin red to suggest
The crystals stimulate synovial release of proteolytic enzymes, including collagenases and other proteases, which degrade cartilage and the rotator cuff in a self-perpetuating destructive cycle

Treatment is largely palliative, using analgesia, anti-inflammatory therapy, joint aspiration, activity modification, and physiotherapy, with surgery including arthroplasty options reserved for selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: In Milwaukee shoulder, basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals within the joint are phagocytosed by synovial lining cells, which respond by secreting matrix metalloproteinases and other proteolytic enzymes. These enzymes degrade articular cartilage and the rotator cuff tendons; the resulting cuff deficiency allows the humeral head to migrate superiorly, and continued crystal shedding perpetuates enzyme release and progressive joint destruction. The effusions are large but contain few inflammatory cells, which helps distinguish the condition from septic or highly inflammatory arthritis.
additionalInvestigations: Joint aspiration showing a large, blood-tinged, low-cell-count effusion, with culture to exclude infection
Alizarin red staining or electron microscopy to suggest or confirm BCP crystals, which are non-birefringent on polarised light
Radiographs showing glenohumeral destruction and superior humeral head migration
MRI or ultrasound to define the rotator cuff tear
Cross-sectional CT for bony destruction and surgical planning
Synovial fluid cell count and Gram stain to differentiate from sepsis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive joint destruction with loss of function
Features that could indicate septic arthritis superimposed on a destroyed joint
reference.prognosis: The condition is typically progressive with a limited response to medical treatment; joint destruction and functional impairment tend to continue, so management is largely aimed at symptom control, with surgery considered only in selected patients because rotator cuff deficiency complicates reconstruction.
pitfalls: Mistaking the large, low-inflammatory effusion for a benign process, or conversely over-diagnosing sepsis
Failing to detect the BCP crystals because they are non-birefringent
Overlooking the massive rotator cuff tear that drives the deformity
Assuming a standard arthroplasty will behave as it would in routine osteoarthritis, when cuff deficiency alters the options and outcome
